newsitem.title: MEXICO: U.S. drug czar warns of Latam drug use problem.
newsitem.headline: U.S. drug czar warns of Latam drug use problem.

text.p: U.S. drug czar Barry McCaffrey warned on Wednesday that many Latin American cities faced worse drug use problems than cities in the United States.

"The drug problem in Rio (de Janeiro), the drug problem in Caracas, the drug problem in Bogota is in many ways far more intense than in Miami, Detroit and San Diego," McCaffrey told the American Chamber of Commerce in Mexico City.
"It's something for all of us to recognise because it underscores the requirement for multinational cooperation," he said in a response to a question.

U.S. officials are hoping to use growing drug consumption problems in Latin America to galvanise governments there to clamp down harder on production and trafficking of narcotics to the United States.

A joint U.S.-Mexican "drug threat assessment" issued on Tuesday said "Mexico recognises that the problem of consumption and dependence is increasing, calling for development of prevention and rehabilitation strategies to address it."

At the same time, officials have been at pains during a visit to Mexico City this week by President Bill Clinton to concede the Latin American point that the vast U.S. demand for drugs has fuelled the trafficking problem.
Clinton, in an address to the Mexican people on Wednesday, noted that the United States, with some 5 percent of the world's population, accounted for about one third of the world's cocaine use.
McCaffrey quoted from the joint report as saying that the number of cocaine users in the United States was "steadily and inexorably dropping" from some 5.7 million in 1985 to 1.5 million in 1995.
But he conceded that drug use -- mainly of marijuana -- among young people aged 12-20 had risen since 1991.
The report had few figures for drug use in Mexico but said that some 1.6 million of the 12- to 65-year-old urban population -- or about 3.9 percent -- admitted having used illegal drugs.

The 2,000-mile (3,200-km) U.S.-Mexican border is the main transit point for drugs coming from South America and Mexico itself, leading to growing U.S. pressure in recent years on the Mexicans to crack down on the country's powerful drug cartels.
The report, however, played down the extent to which drug money had corrupted the Mexican government despite the firing of the country's anti-narcotics chief in February on drug corruption charges.
The 97-page study admitted that corruption was widespread in the judicial and law enforcement system, undermining anti-drug efforts and diminishing public confidence.

But, it said: "Drug-trafficking organisations are far from exercising political control; despite cases of public officials involved in corruption, institutions retain the capacity to act effectively against drug trafficking."

In his remarks at the Chamber of Commerce, McCaffrey conceded there was widespread concern at the State Department's annual "certification," or assessment, of foreign countries' anti-drug cooperation, which is required by the U.S. Congress.

"There is an enormous bubble of anxiety, of distress at what's perceived to be an intrusion in the national sovereignty concerns of our hemispheric partners, and to that extent it's been unhelpful," he said.

McCaffrey referred to moves afoot in Congress to amend the process, but suggested that in the case of Mexico the controversial issue could soon be "submerged" by the anti-drug alliance the two countries are seeking to forge.
In similar vein, Clinton declared in his speech on Wednesday: "The battle against drugs must unite our people, not divide them."
